# THE BOOK OF RUTH — passage digests (map-authored; 14 passages, in story order)

**Ruth 1:1–5** — The famine, the family's sojourn, and the emptying of the household
The passage opens wide, on a whole era, then narrows fast to one family's exile and its slow stripping-away. It moves step by step: famine at home, the move to a foreign land, a household of four named, the father's death, the two sons marrying foreign women, about ten years passing on foreign soil, and at last both sons dead. What weighs on the passage is the shrinking: a whole family of four narrows down, loss by loss, to one grieving woman, alone in a foreign land. The question it leaves hanging is whether anything of this family — its name, its line, its future — can outlast the one woman still standing.
Scenes: Famine and exile to Moab; Death of Elimelech; Marriages and time passing; Deaths of the sons.

**Ruth 1:6–14** — The return road begins; Naomi urges her daughters-in-law back; Orpah turns, Ruth clings
The passage moves from a single piece of news into a journey, and from the journey into an argument on the road that comes in two waves. Naomi hears that YHWH has given bread to his people back in Judah; she gets up and starts home with both daughters-in-law. On the road she stops twice and tries to send them back. The first time she does it with a blessing in YHWH's name — two things she asks for them: hesed (loyal, covenant kindness) and rest. The second time she argues them out of it: she has no more sons in her, she is too old for a husband, and the hand of YHWH has turned against her. The whole movement is a parting the daughters fight; in the end the company breaks in two when Orpah kisses Naomi and turns for home while Ruth holds on to her and will not let go.
Scenes: Hearing and setting out; First appeal and refusal; Second appeal and the split.

**Ruth 1:15–18** — Naomi's last appeal; Ruth's vow; Naomi's silence
The passage moves from Naomi's last try to send Ruth away, through Ruth's binding herself to Naomi for good, to Naomi's silence. Naomi points to Orpah, who has gone back, as the example Ruth should follow. Ruth answers with one long speech that ties herself to Naomi in six steps and seals it with an oath calling down a curse on herself if she breaks it. Naomi sees how set Ruth is, and stops speaking. What carries the passage is the turn from being torn apart to being bound together in a way that cannot be undone — all of it done inside a single speech. The question it leaves is whether Ruth's spoken bond to Naomi — to her people, to her God, to the very ground she will die on — will hold through everything the rest of the book brings.
Scenes: Naomi's last appeal; Ruth's vow; Naomi's silence.

**Ruth 1:19–22** — Naomi and Ruth arrive in Bethlehem; the women of the town react; Naomi renames herself Mara
The passage moves from arrival to silence. Naomi and Ruth reach Bethlehem; the whole town is stirred; the women can hardly believe it is Naomi. When they ask, she answers with a grief-stricken speech in front of them all: she will not be called by her own name, asks to be called Mara — "bitter" — and lays her suffering, twice each, on YHWH and on Shaddai. Then the narrator closes the scene, naming Ruth the Moabite and setting the arrival right at the start of the barley harvest. What weighs on the passage is the gap between what the town expects of Naomi's homecoming and the broken woman she says she has become. The question it leaves hanging is whether the harvest the narrator names at v.22 will answer the lament she has just spoken.
Scenes: Arrival, city stirred, women's question; Naomi's renaming lament; Narrator-frame close: return; Ruth-the-Moabitess; barley-harvest setting.

**Ruth 2:1–7** — Boaz introduced as kinsman; Ruth's gleaning initiative; her chance arrival in Boaz's portion; the foreman's report
The passage moves from a quiet aside by the narrator into a scene out in the fields. The narrator stops at v.1 to introduce Boaz before he does anything. Ruth asks Naomi if she may go and glean, and Naomi lets her. She goes out, gleans, and happens to end up in Boaz's field — and the narrator tells it so you can't quite tell whether it was luck or God's quiet hand. Boaz comes out and greets his reapers in the LORD's name. He asks the man over them whose young woman this is, and the man reports who she is and how she has worked. What weighs on the passage is the gap between what the audience knows and what the people in the story know: the audience has just been told that here is the kinsman who could rescue Elimelech's line, while Ruth and Boaz have not yet so much as met. The question it leaves hanging is whether this chance landing in Boaz's field will turn into his noticing her.
Scenes: Narrator introduces Boaz; Ruth's gleaning initiative; Field arrival; chance in Boaz's portion; Boaz arrives; greeting exchange; Boaz asks the foreman; the foreman reports.

**Ruth 2:8-16** — Boaz speaks to Ruth in the field: instructions, blessing, meal, and harvester protocol
The passage moves through four steps. Boaz tells Ruth to stay in his field, where he will keep her safe. Ruth asks why she, a foreigner, has been shown such favor. Boaz tells her he has heard all she did for her mother-in-law, and blesses her, asking God to shelter her under his wings. The two share a meal with plenty to spare. Then Boaz tells his harvesters to make her gleaning easy. The shape is two sets of instructions wrapped around a center of being noticed and blessed. What weighs on the passage is the gap between who Ruth is — a foreigner, a gleaner — and the welcome she is given: favor, food, safety, blessing. The question it leaves hanging is whether all this care points to something more than enough food for one day.
Scenes: Boaz's first address to Ruth; Ruth's question, Boaz's recital and blessing, Ruth's response; The meal; Boaz's instructions to the young men.

**Ruth 2:17-23** — The gleaning brought home and the redeemer named
The passage moves from the field to home, and then out across a whole season. Ruth gleans until evening, beats out what she gathered, and it comes to about an ephah of barley — a heavy load for one day. She carries it into town, her mother-in-law sees how much there is, and Ruth hands her the food left over from her own meal. Naomi asks where she gleaned and blesses the man who took notice of her — not yet knowing his name. When Ruth names him — Boaz — Naomi blesses him by YHWH, whose hesed (loyal, covenant kindness) has not let go of the living or the dead, and tells Ruth the man is near to them, one of their redeemers (a near relative who can step in for a dead man's family, land, and name). Ruth adds what Boaz said about staying close to his workers; Naomi counsels her to go out with his young women. Ruth does, gleaning to the end of the barley and wheat harvests, and stays living with her mother-in-law. What weighs on the passage is the turn from food to hope: a day's gleaning becomes the first sign that the family's rescue may have a name. The question it leaves hanging is what will come of this kinship now that Naomi has seen it.
Scenes: Gleaning finished, beaten out, and measured; The gleaning carried home; the leftover handed over; Questions, the name, two blessings, the redeemer named, and counsel; Through both harvests, at home with Naomi.

**Ruth 3:1-5** — Naomi's plan for rest; Ruth's total consent
The passage is one quiet exchange that turns the book from provision to permanence. Naomi opens with a question that is really a promise: shall I not seek for you a resting place (manoach — the secure home a married woman has), so that it may be well with you? She names the means in the next breath: Boaz, our kinsman, the man whose young women Ruth worked beside — and tonight he is winnowing barley at the threshing floor. Then the instructions, step by step: wash, anoint yourself, put on your garments, go down to the floor; stay unknown to the man until he has finished eating and drinking; mark the place where he lies; go in, uncover the place of his feet, and lie down. The plan ends not with its goal but with a handoff: he will tell you what to do. Ruth answers with everything at once: all that you say I will do. What weighs on the passage is what is not said — the plan stops at the man's feet and never names marriage, and the risk to a foreign widow alone at night at the floor is left entirely unspoken. The question it leaves hanging is what will happen in the dark between the lying down and the telling.
Scenes: The plan spoken; The consent.

**Ruth 3:6-13** — The threshing-floor night: the wing asked for, the redeemer named, the oath
The passage walks Naomi's plan into the dark and out the other side, changed. Ruth goes down to the floor and does all her mother-in-law commanded. Boaz eats and drinks, his heart is good, and he lies down at the end of the grain heap; she comes softly, uncovers the place of his feet, and lies down. At half of the night the man trembles, twists — and there is a woman lying at his feet. He asks who she is. She answers with her name and more than the plan gave her: I am Ruth your servant — spread your wing over your servant, for you are a redeemer. The plan had said he would tell her what to do; instead she tells him. Boaz answers with a blessing — blessed are you of YHWH, my daughter — and calls this her last hesed (loyal, covenant kindness), better than the first: she has not gone after the young men, poor or rich. He quiets her fear, gives back her own words from the plan's first scene — all that you say I will do for you — and gives the reason: the whole gate of my people knows you are a woman of worth. Then the turn no one planned for: truly I am a redeemer — but there is a redeemer nearer than I. He sets the morning's protocol — if he redeems you, good, let him redeem; if he does not want to, I will redeem you myself — and seals it with the oath: as YHWH lives. Lie down until the morning. What weighs on the passage is how much hangs in the dark between two careful people — desire, law, honor, and a third man's prior claim — and the question it leaves hanging is which redeemer the morning will give her.
Scenes: Down to the floor; the uncovering; Midnight: the startle, the question, the request; Boaz's answer: blessing, pledge, the nearer redeemer, the oath.

**Ruth 3:14-18** — The nameless dawn: six measures home, and sit still
The passage carries the night home and sets the story down to wait. Ruth lies at the place of his feet until morning and rises before one person could recognize another; Boaz says the night's one rule out loud — let it not be known that the woman came to the floor. Then the parting gift: hold out the cloak you are wearing; he measures six measures of barley into it and lays it on her, and he goes into the town. At home, her mother-in-law asks the strange question of the morning — who are you, my daughter? — and Ruth tells her all that the man did for her, and shows the rest: these six measures of barley he gave me, for he said, do not go empty to your mother-in-law. Naomi reads the gift and the man at once: sit still, my daughter, until you know how the matter falls — for the man will not rest unless he has finished the matter today. What weighs on the passage is how much now moves outside the women's reach: the night went unseen, the gift speaks for the man, and the matter is in his hands. The question it leaves hanging is the one Naomi tells Ruth to sit inside: how the matter will fall.
Scenes: The dawn at the floor: the secrecy word and the six measures; Home: the question, the report, and "sit still".

**Ruth 4:1-8** — The gate: the non-name, the field before Ruth, and the sandal
The passage is the morning Naomi promised: the man does not rest. Boaz goes up to the gate and sits down — and behold, the redeemer of whom he spoke is passing. He calls him to turn aside and sit, naming him with a non-name — friend So-and-so — and seats ten men of the town's elders. Then the matter, laid out in two stages. First the field: the portion of our brother Elimelech, which Naomi, back from the fields of Moab, is selling — buy it before those seated and before the elders of my people; if you will redeem, redeem; if not, tell me, for there is no one besides you, and I am after you. The man says: I will redeem. Then the second stage: on the day you buy the field from Naomi's hand, you also acquire Ruth the Moabite, the wife of the dead, to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance. And the redeemer turns back: I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I ruin my own inheritance — you take my right of redemption. The narrator pauses to explain the old way in Israel — for redeeming and for exchanging, a man drew off his sandal and gave it to his fellow; this was the attestation. So the redeemer says to Boaz, buy it for yourself — and draws off his sandal. What weighs on the passage is the order of the telling: the field first, Ruth second — the disclosure staged so that the claim that drew the man in is the one he cannot keep. The question it leaves hanging for one more scene is the word no one has yet said over the bargain: a blessing, a name, a future.
Scenes: The gate convened: the passer-by and the ten; The first stage: the field, and "I will redeem"; The second stage: Ruth named, and the decline; The custom told, and the sandal drawn.

**Ruth 4:9-12** — You are witnesses this day: the names spoken and the gate's blessing
The passage is the book's record made public. Boaz turns from the sandal to the whole assembly and declares what he has done: you are witnesses today that I have bought all that was Elimelech's, and all that was Chilion's and Mahlon's, from Naomi's hand — and that I have bought Ruth the Moabite, the wife of Mahlon, to be my wife, to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance, so that the name of the dead is not cut off from his kindred and from the gate of his place; you are witnesses today. After eight verses of careful namelessness at the gate, the dead are named — Elimelech, Chilion, and Mahlon — and Ruth's husband, withheld since the first chapter, is spoken at last: she is the wife of Mahlon. The assembly answers as one: we are witnesses. Then they bless: may YHWH make the woman coming into your house like Rachel and Leah, who together built the house of Israel; do worthily in Ephrathah and call out a name in Bethlehem; and may your house be like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah, from the seed YHWH gives you from this young woman. What weighs on the passage is the turn from law to blessing and from death to a house: the legal act that preserves a dead man's name becomes a prayer for a living line, and the divine name, silent through the whole proceeding, returns in the people's mouths. The question it leaves hanging is the one the blessing names: the seed, the house, the name yet to be born.
Scenes: Boaz's declaration: the purchase, the names, the witnesses; The assembly's witness and blessing.

**Ruth 4:13-17** — Obed: the conception YHWH gives, the women's blessing, the child on Naomi's lap
The passage is the book's emptiness reversed. Boaz takes Ruth, she becomes his wife, he comes to her — and YHWH gives her conception, and she bears a son. After a book of human acts — gleaning, plans, a night, a gate — the second of the story's only two direct acts of God falls here: the LORD gives the child. The neighbor-women turn to Naomi, not to the parents, and bless: blessed be YHWH, who has not left you without a redeemer today; may his name be called out in Israel. He will be a restorer of your life and a sustainer of your old age — for your daughter-in-law, who loves you, who is better to you than seven sons, has borne him. Naomi takes the child, sets him on her bosom, and becomes his nurse. And the women of the neighborhood call out a name, saying a son has been born to Naomi — and they name him Obed; he is the father of Jesse, the father of David. What weighs on the passage is the turn from death to a living name and from empty to full: the woman who came back saying YHWH had emptied her now holds a child the women call hers, and the line everyone feared was cut off has its name spoken into Israel. The question the book leaves is the one the last line answers past the story's own horizon: where this small, redeemed line is going.
Scenes: The marriage, the gift, the birth; The women's blessing to Naomi; The child on Naomi's lap; the naming.

**Ruth 4:18-22** — The generations of Perez: ten names to David
The passage is the book's last word and its widest: a ten-name line of descent. These are the generations of Perez. Perez fathered Hezron, Hezron fathered Ram, Ram fathered Amminadab, Amminadab fathered Nahshon, Nahshon fathered Salmon, Salmon fathered Boaz, Boaz fathered Obed, Obed fathered Jesse, and Jesse fathered David. The list begins where the elders' blessing pointed — Perez, son of Judah and Tamar — and ends on the name the whole book has been quietly traveling toward: David. What weighs on the passage is its claim, made entirely by arrangement: the small Bethlehem household of a widow and a foreign daughter-in-law stands in the direct line of the king. The story's redeemed child, Obed, is the seventh name and the hinge — Boaz before him, Jesse and David after. The question the book answers here, without a sentence of comment, is the one it has carried under everything: where this rescue was going.
Scenes: The generations of Perez.

## PRESERVATION NOTES — the book's withholdings (HARD CONSTRAINTS, union of all passages)
- [P01] R3 (CROSS_OCCURRENCE_INTRA_PERICOPE): REQUIRED keep-image. Both occurrences must render the same residual-survival verb frame so the rhyme is audible. The first occurrence (1:3) establishes the frame; the second (1:5) completes it. Do not vary the rendering between the two.
- [P01] R5 (CUMULATIVE_LOSS_LISTING_REQUIRED_FORM): REQUIRED keep-image. Single-phrase compression must survive. The reverse-natural-order (children before husband) must be preserved. Do not split into separate sentences if the target language permits the single-phrase form.
- [P01] R6 (STRUCTURAL_ABSENCE_OF_DIVINE_AGENCY): YHWH is not named as agent of any event in P01. The withholding is structural and intentional; it contrasts with the first divine action at 1:6 in P02. Reconstructor must not assign divine causation.
- [P01] R7 (STRUCTURAL_ABSENCE_OF_GRIEF): The narrator reports each death in a single brief clause. No grief, no mourning ritual, no successor is named. The compression carries the weight. Reconstruction must not add grief language not present in the source.
- [P01] R10 (WITHHELD_PAIRING_PER_SOURCE_DISCIPLINE): The source text does not pair the wives with their husbands at 1:4. Pairing is disclosed at 4:10. The MEANING_COORDINATES preserves the withholding via wife_taken: B? in P9 marriage_components. Reconstructor must not infer or state the pairing here.
- [P02] R1 (STRUCTURAL_DIVINE_AGENCY_FIRST_NAMED): First non-NONE agent_named in the pilot. Structural inverse of P01's three NONE-agent events (P01 P2 famine, P7 Elimelech's death, P12 sons' deaths). Reconstructor must preserve the divine subject as the agent of bread-provision.
- [P02] R3 (STRUCTURAL_DIVINE_ATTRIBUTION_IN_LAMENT): Naomi's lament-frame ascription: 'the hand of YHWH has gone out against me.' Same divine subject as P2, opposite valence in Naomi's perception. Reconstructor must not soften or generalize the attribution; it is Naomi's voice naming YHWH as the agent of her bitterness.
- [P02] R5 (WITHHELD_PAIRING_PER_SOURCE_DISCIPLINE): Naomi's hesed-blessing grounding clause references the daughters' prior hesed 'toward the dead and toward me' without disclosing which daughter-in-law's hesed went to which deceased husband. Pairing remains withheld per P01-D2 carry-forward. Disclosure deferred to 4:10.
- [P02] R14 (STRUCTURAL_CONTRAST): Two parallel acts on one verse define the divergence of the two daughters' paths. Orpah's act closes her arc in the book; Ruth's act opens the rest of the book's trajectory. The contrast must remain visible in reconstruction.
- [P03] R1 (VOW_AND_BINDING_BEYOND_DEATH): First oath-scene in the pilot. Six successive bindings (path, lodging, people, God, death-place, burial-place) closed by the canonical self-curse oath formula 'may YHWH do thus to me and worse'. The conditional 'if death itself separates between me and you' binds Ruth past her own death — the condition can only fail through death. Reconstructor must preserve the six-step ladder as six bindings (do not collapse 'people'+'God' or 'death'+'burial'), preserve the closing self-curse formula without softening, and preserve the binds-past-death structural force of the conditional.
- [P03] R3 (FIGURE_FIRST_OCCURRENCE): REQUIRED keep-image. Extends the binding past life; both halves of the death-and-burial commitment must land structurally distinct ('where you die I will die' is one binding; 'and there I will be buried' is a separate binding). The two halves must render as a clear pair, not as a single conflated death-burial binding. Within-pericope pair: opens at v.17a first half, closes at v.17a second half.
- [P03] R4 (FIGURE_FIRST_OCCURRENCE): REQUIRED keep-image. The canonical Hebrew self-curse oath formula 'may YHWH do thus to me and worse' (כֹּה יַעֲשֶׂה יְהוָה לִי וְכֹה יוֹסִיף). Do not soften. High terminological-consistency requirement across the book (will recur at 3:13 in Boaz's oath at the threshing floor) and across the Hebrew canon (recurs at 1 Sam 3:17; 14:44; 20:13; 2 Sam 3:9; 19:14; 1 Kgs 2:23; 2 Kgs 6:31). Reconstruction must preserve the divine-name invocation and the open-ended 'and more' clause.
- [P03] R5 (STRUCTURAL_DIVINE_NAMING_FIRST_ON_OUTSIDER_LIPS): First time the divine name YHWH appears on Ruth's lips in the book. The named divine subject was last heard in P02 from Naomi's voice (provider at 1:6, hand-against at 1:13); P03 places the name on the Moabite outsider's lips for the first time. Structurally significant for T6 (YHWH-at-work) and T5 (Moabite-outsider-incorporation). Reconstructor must preserve YHWH-named at v.17, not generic-deity.
- [P03] R7 (SIGNIFICANT_ABSENCE): The narrator does not label Ruth with the Moabite epithet anywhere in P03. At the moment of Ruth's verbal covenant-binding to Naomi's people and God, the narrator does not re-assert the ethnic boundary. The withholding is structurally significant for T5 (Moabite-outsider-incorporation). Reconstructor must not insert the Moabite epithet inside or around the vow; later pericopes (P05, P07, P11, P12) will resume the epithet where the narrator does.
- [P03] R10 (SIGNIFICANT_ABSENCE): Narrator at v.18 reports Naomi seeing Ruth's determination and ceasing speech to her, but does not report Naomi's interior response. No agreement, no blessing, no acceptance, no rejection, no further word from Naomi inside the pericope. The narrator gives interior access only to Ruth's resolve (via the hithpael participle מִתְאַמֶּצֶת), not to Naomi's response. The withholding is structurally open and load-bearing. Reconstructor must not fill the silence with Naomi's interior, with an inferred acceptance, or with a continuation past v.18.
- [P04] R1 (STRUCTURAL_DIVINE_NAME_FIRST_OCCURRENCE): The archaic-poetic divine name Shaddai appears for the first time in the book at v.20 ('Shaddai has dealt very bitterly') and again at v.21 ('Shaddai has done evil to me'). Distinct from YHWH; pairs and alternates with YHWH across the two verses. Reconstructor must preserve Shaddai as a distinct divine-name (not flatten to a single divine-name across the four attributions).
- [P04] R2 (STRUCTURAL_DIVINE_NAME_DOUBLING_PATTERN): Naomi names Shaddai twice (v.20 bittering; v.21 evil-doing) and YHWH twice (v.21 brought-back-empty; v.21 testified-against). Four divine attributions in two verses. The Shaddai-YHWH alternation is structurally significant: Shaddai for the bittering and harm; YHWH for the return-empty and the courtroom testimony. Reconstructor must preserve all four; do not collapse to a single divine-name.
- [P04] R3 (FIGURE_FIRST_OCCURRENCE): REQUIRED keep-image. Naomi refuses her name Naomi (meaning 'sweet') and proposes Mara (meaning 'bitter'). The substitution names her experience and refuses her given identity. The reconstructor must preserve both halves: the refusal and the proposal. The narrator does not adopt the new name (see R9); the proposal stands as Naomi's voice without becoming her actual referential form going forward.
- [P04] R5 (FIGURE_FIRST_OCCURRENCE): REQUIRED keep-image. 'I went out full, and YHWH brought me back empty' — first antithetical state-word pair in the book. The pair is structurally placed across the journey-arc (out = full; back = empty). The Hebrew empty-handed lexeme riqam (רֵיקָם) is specifically the antonym Naomi uses; it recurs at P10 in the structural answer. Reconstructor must preserve both halves of the antithesis and the journey-arc placement.
- [P04] R9 (STRUCTURAL_NON_ADOPTION_OF_PROPOSED_RENAMING): Naomi proposes 'Mara' at v.20 and reinforces the refusal of 'Naomi' at v.21. The narrator immediately uses 'Naomi' again at v.22. The non-adoption is structurally significant: the narrator does not endorse Naomi's self-renaming. Reconstructor must encode the proposal as Naomi's voice without applying the new name in narrator voice or in later references. Naomi continues to be called Naomi for the rest of the book.
- [P04] R10 (REFERENTIAL_FORM_REACTIVATION_AFTER_WITHHOLDING): The narrator returns to the Moabite epithet at the public-arrival moment in Bethlehem. The structural counterpart to P03 R7 SIGNIFICANT_ABSENCE (which recorded the withholding at the vow moment). Reconstructor must restore the epithet at v.22 — Ruth publicly enters Israel as the Moabitess. The withholding-and-reactivation pattern is structurally meaningful across the chapter 1 arc.
- [P04] R12 (SIGNIFICANT_ABSENCE): The narrator does not say why the women cannot recognize Naomi. Grief, age, demeanor, appearance are all possible; the narrator withholds. Reconstructor must not fill the cause. The recognition-failure stands as is.
- [P05] R3 (STRUCTURAL_AUDIENCE_LEVEL_GAP_AT_S2_DIALOGUE): The narrator introduces Boaz to the audience at v.1 in the parenthetical, then immediately moves to Ruth-Naomi interior dialogue at v.2 where Naomi does not name Boaz, does not suggest a kinsman, does not warn or bless. The audience-knows-character-doesn't gap is structurally meaningful — it is the narrator's deliberate setup for the audience to hold the kinship knowledge across the chance-arrival. Reconstructor must not insert Naomi naming or alluding to Boaz at v.2.
- [P05] R4 (STRUCTURAL_PROVIDENCE_WITHOUT_NAMING_AGENT_WITHHELD): REQUIRED keep-image on FIG_0015. The narrator's signature providence-without-naming move: the construction holds ambiguity between coincidence and providence; YHWH is not named as agent. Flattening to plain 'she happened to come' or to plain 'YHWH led her' loses the irony in either direction. Reconstructor must preserve the ambiguity. agent_named: NONE in MEANING_COORDINATES P5; do not infer divine agency.
- [P05] R10 (REFERENTIAL_FORM_REACTIVATION_IN_THIRD_PARTY_VOICE): The carry-forward arc continues: opened P01 v.4 (narrator) → withheld P02-P03 → narrator-voice reactivation P04 v.22 → narrator-epithet at speech-event head P05 v.2 → third-party-voice at P05 v.6 (foreman's 'a Moabite young woman'). The third-party-voice occurrence is structurally significant — the field-community now identifies Ruth by the ethnic epithet, not by name. Reconstructor must preserve the Moabite epithet on the foreman's lips at v.6; the personal name 'Ruth' must not appear in the foreman's voice.
- [P05] R12 (STRUCTURAL_ABSENCE_OF_PROTAGONIST_INTERIOR): The narrator gives Boaz's question to the foreman without any interior-state attribution — no surprise, no recognition, no inclination, no marked emotional weight. The narrator does not say what Boaz notices about Ruth, why he asks, or what he is thinking. Reconstructor must not fill the interior; the question must stand without surrounding interior commentary.
- [P05] R13 (TEXTUAL_CLARITY_FLAG): The Hebrew 'זֶה שִׁבְתָּהּ הַבַּיִת מְעָט' is textually disputed; readings range from 'she has rested only a little in the shelter' to 'she has not rested even for a moment.' Encoded in MEANING_COORDINATES P9 fifth component with textual_clarity_flag: true. Reconstructor must hold the ambiguity open; do not resolve. The PL_HA_BAYIT_FIELD_SHELTER place-code is registered in BCD-DELTA with notes on the textual uncertainty; the syntactic uncertainty is at the proposition-level only.
- [P06] R1 (FIGURE_FIRST_OCCURRENCE): REQUIRED keep-image. The Hebrew word kanaph must render the same way at 2:12 and at 3:9 so the petition lands as an answer to the blessing. Cross-pericope pair opens here.
- [P06] R3 (CROSS_OCCURRENCE_INTRA_PERICOPE): The cluster is distributed structurally across the pericope. Touch at v.9 is reported prior speech; shame at v.15 is bundled with permission-to-glean; rebuke at v.16 is bundled with leave-them. Each member must remain visible in its own structural slot. Do not collapse into a single instruction.
- [P06] R4 (WITHHELD_PAIRING_PER_SOURCE_DISCIPLINE): Boaz says 'after the death of your husband' without naming which son. The pairing Mahlon-Ruth is disclosed at 4:10. P7 uses after_whose_death: B? per P01-D2 carry-forward. Reconstructor must not infer the pairing here.
